name: Salivary glands
func: Make saliva, about 1–1.5 litres a day, which moistens food, starts digesting starch, protects the teeth and fights germs. The three big pairs are the parotid, submandibular and sublingual glands.

levels.kid:
Your **salivary glands** are little factories that make **spit**, or **saliva**. You have three big pairs: one in front of each ear, one under each side of your jaw, and one under your tongue. You also have hundreds of tiny ones all over the inside of your mouth.

When you smell yummy food, or even just think about it, your mouth starts to water. That's your salivary glands getting ready!

Saliva makes food wet and slippery so you can chew and swallow it. It also has a special helper that starts breaking down foods like bread and rice while they're still in your mouth. And it washes your teeth and fights germs, helping to stop cavities.

When you get **mumps**, the glands in front of your ears swell up and your cheeks puff out.
levels.hs:
The three paired **major salivary glands**:
- **Parotid gland**: the largest, sitting in front of and below the ear, wrapped around the back edge of the **mandible** and over the **masseter** muscle. Its duct (**Stensen's or parotid duct**) runs across the masseter, pierces the **buccinator** and opens inside the cheek opposite the **upper second molar**. The **facial nerve** (CN VII) passes right through the gland.
- **Submandibular gland**: under the body of the mandible, wrapping around the back edge of the **mylohyoid** muscle. Its duct (**Wharton's or submandibular duct**) opens beside the **lingual frenulum** under the tongue.
- **Sublingual gland**: the smallest, under the tongue in the floor of the mouth, opening through many small ducts.

Hundreds of **minor salivary glands** are scattered in the lips, cheeks and palate.

Together they make about **1–1.5 litres** of saliva a day. Most resting saliva comes from the submandibular glands; during eating the **parotids** contribute much more. Saliva contains water, electrolytes, **mucins** (for slipperiness), **salivary amylase** (starts breaking down starch), **lingual lipase** (from glands at the back of the tongue), antibacterial **lysozyme**, **lactoferrin** and **IgA** antibodies, and **bicarbonate** to buffer acid and protect tooth enamel.
levels.college:
**Secretion types**: the parotid is almost purely **serous** (watery, enzyme-rich); the submandibular is **mixed** (mostly serous); the sublingual is mixed but mostly **mucous**.

Each gland has **acini** (secretory end-pieces) drained by a duct system: **intercalated ducts** → **striated ducts** → interlobular and excretory ducts. **Myoepithelial cells** around acini contract to squeeze saliva out.

**Nerve supply** is mainly **parasympathetic**, and it's a classic exam topic because of its winding route:
- **Parotid**: **CN IX** → tympanic nerve → lesser petrosal nerve → **otic ganglion** → postganglionic fibres hitchhike on the **auriculotemporal nerve** (V3) to the gland.
- **Submandibular and sublingual**: **CN VII** → **chorda tympani** → joins the **lingual nerve** → **submandibular ganglion** → glands.

Sympathetic fibres from the superior cervical ganglion travel along arteries and produce smaller volumes of thicker, protein-rich saliva.

**Relations that matter**: within the parotid, the **facial nerve** splits into its five branches (temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical), lying superficial to the **retromandibular vein** and **external carotid artery**. The submandibular gland is crossed by the **facial artery**, and its duct is crossed twice by the **lingual nerve** in the floor of the mouth, while the **hypoglossal nerve** runs below it. The **marginal mandibular branch** of the facial nerve runs just over the gland.

The **parotid capsule** is tough and continuous with deep cervical fascia, so swelling inside it is very painful.
levels.phd:
Saliva is made in **two stages**. First, acinar cells secrete a **primary fluid** similar to plasma (isotonic). Acetylcholine on **M3 receptors** raises intracellular calcium, opening apical **TMEM16A (ANO1)** chloride channels and basolateral **calcium-activated potassium** channels. Chloride exits apically, sodium follows between cells, and water follows through **aquaporin-5** water channels. The **NKCC1** cotransporter loads chloride into the cell.

Second, the **striated ducts** modify it: they reabsorb sodium and chloride (via **ENaC** and **CFTR**) and secrete potassium and bicarbonate, but they're relatively **water-impermeable**. The result is **hypotonic** saliva, which helps taste sensitivity. At high flow rates, there's less time for modification, so saliva becomes less hypotonic and richer in bicarbonate.

**Salivary amylase (AMY1)** cleaves α-1,4 glycosidic bonds in starch. Copy number of the **AMY1** gene varies widely between people and correlates with traditionally high-starch diets, a well-studied example of human gene-diet co-evolution.

Saliva also contains **histatins** and **statherins** (antifungal and enamel-protecting), **epidermal growth factor** (aids mucosal healing) and **proline-rich proteins** that form the protective **acquired pellicle** on teeth.

Salivary reflexes: unconditioned (taste and chewing via the solitary nucleus) and conditioned (Pavlov's famous dog experiments). The **superior** and **inferior salivatory nuclei** in the brainstem send parasympathetic output through CN VII and CN IX respectively.

Saliva is increasingly studied as a **diagnostic fluid**: hormone and antibody measurements, viral detection and genomic DNA collection are all done from saliva samples.
levels.expert:
**Exam**: inspect and palpate the parotid region and under the jaw, and use **bimanual palpation** (one finger inside the mouth, one outside) for the submandibular gland and duct. Look for pus or a stone at the duct openings. **Always test facial nerve function** when assessing a parotid lump.

**Stones (sialolithiasis)**: about **80–90% occur in the submandibular gland**, because its saliva is thicker and more alkaline, and its duct runs uphill. The classic sign is **pain and swelling at mealtimes**. Imaging: **ultrasound** first, then CT or **sialendoscopy**, which can also remove stones.

**Infections**: **mumps** (viral parotitis, usually both sides) and **acute bacterial parotitis** (usually *Staphylococcus aureus*, in dehydrated, older or post-operative patients).

**Dry mouth (xerostomia)**: from **Sjögren syndrome** (autoimmune; dry eyes and mouth, anti-Ro/La antibodies, lymphocytic infiltrates on lip biopsy, increased lymphoma risk), radiotherapy to the head and neck, and many medicines with anticholinergic effects. **Drooling (sialorrhoea)** is common in neurological disease such as Parkinson disease, cerebral palsy and ALS, mainly from impaired swallowing; treatment can include **botulinum toxin** injections into the glands.

**Tumours**: about **80% of salivary tumours are in the parotid**, and about 80% of parotid tumours are benign, most often a **pleomorphic adenoma**, followed by **Warthin tumour**. The smaller the gland, the more likely a tumour is malignant. Facial nerve weakness with a parotid lump suggests **malignancy**.

**Surgery**: in **parotidectomy** the surgeon identifies the **facial nerve trunk** (using landmarks like the tragal pointer) and preserves its branches. A late complication is **Frey syndrome** (gustatory sweating): regenerating parasympathetic fibres wire into sweat glands, so the cheek sweats when eating.

keyPoints: Parotid duct opens opposite the upper 2nd molar; facial nerve runs through the gland
Parotid via CN IX (otic ganglion); submandibular/sublingual via CN VII (chorda tympani)
Saliva is hypotonic: ducts reabsorb salt but not water
Most stones are in the submandibular gland
Most salivary tumours are parotid pleomorphic adenomas

test.q: Which gland has the facial nerve running through it?
test.explain: The facial nerve divides into its branches inside the parotid, so parotid surgery must protect it.

test.q: Which gland gets the most salivary stones?
test.explain: Its thicker, alkaline saliva and uphill duct make the submandibular gland the main site of stones.

test.q: The parasympathetic ganglion supplying the parotid gland is the ______ ganglion.
test.explain: CN IX fibres synapse in the otic ganglion, then travel with the auriculotemporal nerve.

choices: Ducts reabsorb sodium and chloride but little water
test.explain: Striated ducts remove sodium and chloride while staying relatively impermeable to water.

test.q: Sweating on the cheek while eating after parotid surgery is ______ syndrome.
test.explain: Frey syndrome happens when regrowing parasympathetic fibres connect to sweat glands in the skin.
